Jerome may be cooling off, but Cam Boozer is heating up: the No. 3 overall pick just shot 50-44-100 for the week and picked up his first career triple-double in a win over the then-unbeaten Portland Trail Blazers (and former Grizzlies star Ja Morant). Nobody can miss a 3. Zech Edey and Isaiah Stewart are almost completely walling off the rim. Grizzlies opponents are taking only 19 shots per game in the restricted area.

The pick-and-roll-heavy scheme Tuomas Iisalo was known for abroad is finally coming together in the NBA. Only the Cleveland Cavaliers have generated more shots out of pick-and-roll than Memphis. Only the Miami Heat and Houston Rockets are scoring more points per possession on those shots. After Iisalo's short-stint rotations caused so much of an uproar last season, Memphis has gotten off to this start with nobody averaging even 32 minutes a game.

Memphis won't be this good forever. They've played a Charmin soft schedule. Eventually, they'll start missing 3s, and Jerome will probably settle somewhere between the MVP frontrunner he was in Week 1 and the far less effective player we saw in Week 2. But all of this winning isn't a fluke. It's not as though their opponents are just missing shots. They're killing the teams that they're playing. Even if 82-0 is unrealistic, a playoff berth certainly feels realistic for a Grizzlies team that is thriving to start the season.

Nobody roots for injuries, but teams certainly benefit from them. We came into the season assuming the Thunder and Spurs were heavy championship favorites. The Thunder are suddenly in peril, and the Rockets beat San Antonio head-to-head in the season's opening week. They have one of the few big men in the NBA in Alperen Sengun who seems genuinely comfortable attacking Victor Wembanyama. He shot 17 of 23 against Wembanyama as the primary defender last season, according to NBA.com tracking data. He just dropped a 29-7-7 on him in Houston's second game of the year. The stars are aligning for the Rockets already.

This isn't purely a matter of circumstance, either. Houston has clearly leveled up with Fred VanVleet back in the fold. They'd likely be standing alongside the Grizzlies in the ranks of the undefeated had Sengun not missed Friday's loss to the Dallas Mavericks. After a year of consternation about their mess of a half-court offense, Houston ranks fourth in the NBA in points per 100 half-court plays thus far this season. They have the NBA's No. 1 overall offense despite barely getting any minutes out Steven Adams so far. Just imagine how easily they'll score with his offensive rebounding in the mix.

The season is far too young to say anything definitively, especially with injuries coming so quickly. For now, at least, Houston should feel relatively safe about outwinning Oklahoma City in the regular season, and it has a one-game lead and a head-to-head victory over San Antonio in its back pocket. The No. 1 seed feels much more attainable to them than it did two weeks ago, and with it would come the easiest possible path to the NBA Finals.

The consensus surrounding Lendeborg as a draft prospect was that, as a 24-year-old on opening night, he would arrive in the NBA as a productive player, but would have limited upside to grow beyond that. He's older than Jonathan Kuminga, after all, so it's not as though his arrival heralded the emergence of yet another timeline. At this rate, though, it might not matter if Lendeborg has already peaked as an NBA player, because the last week suggests he might have arrived in the NBA as a star.

His collegiate career-high in scoring was 30 points. He's topped that figure twice in the last week alone, and it's not as though he's doing that with crazy volume. His season-high in shot attempts (20) is Darius Acuff's season-low. His only bad game of the week came in his hyped rematch with Luka Dončić... a game the Golden State Warriors still managed to win despite Lendeborg claiming he "wet the bed."

Lendeborg's emergence has a chance to be genuinely transformative for Golden State. Suddenly the Warriors have the secondary scorer they need next to Curry. When Jimmy Butler returns, they'll have one of the most physically imposing pairs of forwards in the NBA, helping to offset their size issues at center with Kristaps Porziņģis sidelined. Maybe Lendeborg is even good enough to compel Golden State to attach draft picks to Porziņģis' contract and go make a win-now move. A week ago, the Warriors were winless and limping their way through a hopeless season. They've since won four straight and generated their first real dose of optimism since Butler tore his ACL, and it's almost entirely because of a rookie that somehow slipped out of the top 10 of the draft.

On Monday, the Thunder announced that both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace would have surgeries that could end their seasons. That night, they lost Alex Caruso to a sprained ankle. That's a year's worth of injury news in a night, and then on Friday, it came out Chet Holmgren has a small patellar tendon tear that will require an 8-10 week absence following a "biological" treatment. What exactly that means for his long-term health prospects is unclear.

The Thunder opened the season by avenging their Western Conference Finals loss to the San Antonio Spurs. They followed that up by dispatching the player team that pushed them to the brink in the 2025 playoffs: Nikola Jokić and the Denver Nuggets. They looked like heavy championship favorites.

Now? It's possible that they reached the point of no return on injuries before Halloween, and if they haven't now, they could at any moment. We went from "the Thunder are the best team in the NBA" to "the Thunder could trade their way back into the championship picture" to "does it really make sense for the Thunder to start their luxury tax in this nightmare season?" all in the span of a few days. That last question is still months away from an answer, but the fact that it's even on the table is a testament to just how disastrous the last week or so has been in Oklahoma City.

We have our first reports of an unhappy team in this early season, and it is one of last year's surprise success stories: the Phoenix Suns. On Thursday, Chris Haynes explained that "there is some growing frustration within that locker room for the simple fact that that roster does not have a point guard that can organize that offense."

We should clarify here that the Suns do have a point guard on their roster... they're just not starting him. The Suns are scoring 123.2 points per 100 possessions with Collin Gillespie on the floor... and 106.4 with him off it, according to Cleaning the Glass. Pretty much all of the underlying numbers suggest that simply starting Gillespie over Jalen Green could solve some of these point guard issues. The Suns assist on 76.3% of their baskets with Gillespie on the floor so far this season, but only 54.2% of them with him off it. Devin Booker has a 68.1% true shooting percentage with Gillespie playing and a 51.3% mark without him.

The decision to start Green was a questionable one even before the season started. He wasn't really a part of last season's success. He was a No. 2 overall pick, sure, but that was for a different team. The Suns don't have enough invested in Green to justify the continued usage of these suboptimal lineups. They frankly have too many real problems to continue creating more of them for themselves with suboptimal lineup decisions.

The Suns had a top-10 defense a year ago. They rank 30th early in this season. Their dominant offensive rebounding has slipped to the middle of the pack as well, and even their turnover rate has ticked up a bit. The Suns beat expectations last season because they were disciplined and they played harder than anyone in the league. They've fallen from No. 5 to No. 26 in deflections per game this season, and No. 6 to No. 26 in loose ball recoveries. These aren't the hustle Suns of a year ago, at least thus far. Some of that can be traced back to the players taking on new prominence this season. Green isn't exactly known as a high-energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who has thus far underwhelmed following Phoenix's decision to trade an unprotected first-round pick for him over the summer.

The Suns were the feel-good story of last season. Going from that to the first team to leak displeasure to the press this season is a pretty precipitous drop. A point guard upgrade, internal or external, isn't going to address everything wrong with this team.

The Jazz are actually trying to win for the first time in the Will Hardy era... yet they're playing worse than they did when they were trying to lose. Utah's 1-5 start is the second-worst of Hardy's tenure in Utah, trailing only the six-game losing streak that kicked off their 2024-25 season. Utah's offense -- vaunted for thriving with limited resources at points during the Jazz rebuild -- is scoring fewer points per 100 possessions (105.3) than it did in any full season during the Hardy era.

The loss of the perpetually injury-prone Jaren Jackson Jr. to a torn MCL this week brought several major decisions Utah has made over the past year or so into question. The Jazz gave up three first-round picks to get Jackson on a max deal, and he's thus far given them nine games. They traded Walker Kessler and passed on Cam Boozer in the NBA Draft in part because they had Jackson. Kessler's Lakers are 5-2, and Boozer is competing with Lendeborg to become the early Rookie of the Year frontrunner. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson has been by far the least impressive of the top four picks in June's draft thus far and was even benched down the stretch of an overtime loss to the San Antonio Spurs.

We're six games into the season. It is much too early to panic over the state of the Jazz. But after punting four full seasons to get where they are now, Utah certainly expected more than it has gotten thus far, and with Jackson injured, there's no telling when or if the Jazz will be able to turn things around.

#2580. Tarik Skubal landing spots: Predicting new home for two-time Cy Young winner, the offseason's best free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. I don't think the owners win the fight for a salary cap, but there'll be enough push from the Dodgers' end before the CBA talks shut down free agency to snatch up all the talent they can to get his contract grandfathered before a new agreement.

#2578. Seahawks vs. Bears prediction: Caleb Williams faces toughest test yet in Seattle defense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the Week 8 edition of "Monday Night Football," the Seattle Seahawks host the Chicago Bears. Seattle enters this game fresh off a victory over the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs, snapping a two-game losing skid. The Seahawks' defense is settling in and once again looks like one of the best units in the league, but faces one of its toughest tests of the season on Monday night.

Chicago enters having won both of its games since starting quarterback Caleb Williams returned from injury, improving to 5-2 in the process. The Bears have looked like one of the best offenses in the NFL whenever Williams has been on the field, but they, too, face arguably their toughest test of the season on Monday evening.

Will Seattle make it back-to-back wins, or will the Bears ruin their evening with a road upset?

Chicago has scored, 59, 31 and 30 points in the three Caleb Williams starts that were not played against the Minnesota Vikings in a driving rainstorm. The Bears piled up 552, 368 and 405 yards in those three games, and turned the ball over only twice in those contests.

For the season (including the game against Minnesota), Williams has completed 71% of his passes at an average of 8.2 yards per attempt, both of which are career-high figures. He has thrown five touchdowns against one interception and rushed 24 times for 128 yards and two additional scores.

Williams has generally thrown short passes, with an average depth of throw of only 7.0 yards, according to Tru Media. Despite that, he has created explosive passing plays at the third-highest rate in the league (10.7% of dropbacks). That's thanks in large part to the fact that the Bears are averaging 6.4 yards after catch per completion on his throws, the fourth-best mark in the league.

The Seahawks, though, limit YAC as well as just about any team in football. They've allowed only 4.5 yards after catch per completion, which ranks third-best in the NFL. They play shell coverages a lot of the time, and they rally to the ball and tackle as well in the secondary as anybody. Their defensive backs and linebackers rarely miss opportunities to bring ball-carriers to the ground.

The Bears generally want to run the ball more often than almost any team in the league, with a 48.7% rush rate, according to Tru Media. The Seahawks are elite at stopping the run, however, as we saw last week against Kenneth Walker III. D'Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson will have their work cut out for them here, even against a defense that plays a lot of nickel and dime and doesn't load the box.

The Chicago offensive line will have to do a lot of work to move Seattle's defensive front off the ball, which has proven extremely difficult for opposing lines this year.

Seattle's offense is built almost entirely around the exploits of superstar wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba. JSN leads the NFL with 867 receiving yards, 43 receiving first downs and eight receiving touchdowns. He has been targeted on 36.3% of the team's pass attempts, which ranks as the No. 1 mark in the NFL. So does his 33.9% targets-per-route-run rate, which is narrowly ahead of CeeDee Lamb's.

Smith-Njigba has more receptions than the next three closest players on the Seahawks: AJ Barner, Cooper Kupp and Rashid Shaheed combined for 53. His 867 yards are also considerably more than the 562 that trio has combined as well. They are ancillary pieces at best, and typically they are scarcely involved in the offense. Shaheed is also out on Monday night, which means the secondary options will be even more limited than usual.

The Bears, like everyone else in the league, do not have anyone who can cover Smith-Njigba. It's not possible. The best chance to limit him is to get to Sam Darnold and force hurried decisions that lead to turnovers. Darnold, despite missing time due to injury, leads the NFL with eight interceptions.

Under pressure, he has been dreadful, completing only 26 of 66 passes for 331 yards, two touchdowns and four picks. He ranks second-to-last in the league in EPA per dropback on pressured plays, per Tru Media. If the Bears can get into his face, they can force him into mistakes and flip the game on its head.

Something that will help them in that effort is the arrival of defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who is a game wrecker on the interior. Simmons is among the league leaders in both pressures and sacks when lined up inside. He'll have to deal with what is now one of the best guard duos in the league in Quenton Nelson and Grey Zabel, and Simmons could also see his snaps limited in his first game with his new team. (Nelson is likely to play a full complement in his Seattle debut, given how reluctant teams are to rotate offensive linemen.)

The Seattle running game should get a boost from the expected returns of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price. Charbonnet hasn't played all season after tearing his ACL during last year's Super Bowl run, while Price has been out since Week 3 with a chest injury. The combination of Emanuel Wilson and George Holani has largely been ineffective, and even if Charbonnet and Price can generate slightly below-average efficiency, they'll represent an improvement over the incumbent duo. The Bears have given up an average of 4.4 yards per carry this season, which ranks 23rd in the league.

Seattle's defense is looking like the unit we expected it to be coming into the year. The Seahawks just shut down Kenneth Walker last week; they should be able to do the same to D'Andre Swift. That puts the entire game on Williams' right shoulder. He can handle that, of course, but it's incredibly difficult to do against Mike Macdonald's unit. That's especially true if the Seahawks get Price and Charbonnet back in the lineup at running back and can run the ball with some degree of success. Pick the Seahawks to take care of business at home.

#2577. Ranking NBA injuries so far: Why Anthony Edwards' absence is a bigger blow than any single OKC injury

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA's "unprecedented" injury crisis to start the season has everyone searching for answers, even though it's obvious: Shorten the season and/or the games themselves. FIBA games last 40 minutes, not 48, and the pace at which these players are asked to play and the ground they have to cover in a way more spaced-out game, to say nothing of the force they're creating as bigger and more powerful athletes than the league has ever seen, is going to continue breeding injuries.

We'll see what, if anything, the NBA decides to do about it. My guess is the almighty dollar will continue to win. The league wants as many games as possible for maximum revenue -- both in-arena and through TV contracts -- and if the players have to drop their salaries for playing fewer games, well, it's hard to see that happening either.

And so we're left to deal with a league that is quickly being defined as much by the players who aren't playing as those who are. It sucks. No other way to put it. And it's having a major impact on the competitive landscape -- which is what we're here to look at in this article.

Below I have ranked the 10 most significant injuries this season in terms of how much impact they will have on the postseason seeding race. I'm not going to look ahead to how it might affect the playoffs as an extension of that, because the playoffs are a different beast where matchups are paramount. We will look at the postseason health status of the relevant teams as we get closer to that point.

But as seeding races go, what's happening right now is just as important as what happens later in the season. The games all count the same.

This is all subject to change as more injuries, unfortunately, are likely to arise, and timetables could be extended for those teams are already dealing with. But given the information we have at this moment, and with as realistic a projection as possible, here's where I come out on the injury-impact rankings.

*NOTE: I have not included any of the injuries that existed prior to the season starting. We knew about those and accounted for them in our season outlooks. So no Jimmy Butler, Kristaps Porzingis, Kon Kneuppel, Coby White (who's expected back Monday night) or Brandon Ingram, among others.

Jalen Williams' injury is obviously worse, but in terms of impact on their respective teams, Minnesota is facing a bigger uphill challenge without Edwards through Christmas than the Thunder are without Williams for the whole season. Edwards was off to a torrid start, averaging 33.3 points and leading the league in 3-pointers at the time of injury.

Edwards and LaMelo Ball were seriously vibing, but Edwards' absence exacerbates Ball's inefficiency and puts a lot more on his shoulders as a scorer. So far, he hasn't been up to the task. In his first game without Edwards, Ball had eight points on 3-of-11 shooting in a loss to the Warriors. On Saturday, he had 10 points on 2-of-10 shooting in a loss to San Antonio.

For the season, Ball is averaging just north of 14 points and six assists, far cries from his typical production. He's shooting 39% overall. He's 9 for his last 32 from 3. Chris Finch says his point guard is getting "fouled all over the floor," but that's a desperate plea by a coach who knows his team could be in a serious hole by the time Edwards gets back if Ball doesn't pick it up significantly, to say nothing of the possibility that this knee issue continues to bother Edwards even after his return.

Unlike the situation with Williams in Oklahoma City, where they at least have a viable offensive replacement in Ajay Mitchell, there is nobody in Minnesota who can provide anything close to Ant's MVP-level production, and two months is a hell of a long time in this Western Conference. The Wolves started out 3-1 with Edwards. They're 1-2 so far without him.

How is a season-ending injury as gruesome as this one not No. 1 on a list like this? Because Williams played in just 33 games last season and the Thunder still won 64. They went 39-10 without Williams in the regular season and 8-2 in the playoffs.

Yes, the Thunder were much deeper on the wing last year. They lost Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe this summer, and now Cason Wallace is probably going to miss at least the rest of the regular season, too. But they still have Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain to cover for Williams offensively and Alex Caruso (when he gets back from his sprained ankle) on defense. It's not optimal, obviously, but having the back-to-back MVP gives OKC a lot of leeway.

Holmgren being out 8-10 weeks is actually what tips this Thunder boat on its side, but given that it's not season-ending, there's at least a light at the end of the tunnel. Williams almost certainly isn't coming back this year, and you have to at least wonder if he'll ever be the same moving forward with his career. This is the same injury Gordon Hayward suffered, and though Williams is younger, Hayward was an All-NBA level player at the time and was never close to the same again; he managed just 318 more career games before calling it quits.

If Wallace were healthy, the Williams injury, awful as it is, wouldn't have been quite as significant, and if Williams hadn't gone down, Wallace's absence wouldn't have hit quite as hard. But these two blows coming at the same time makes both of them exponentially worse.

Williams is a better player than Wallace and is almost certainly done for the season, whereas Wallace could at least come back for the playoffs. Even with all these injuries, it's still hard to imagine the Thunder not making postseason play as long as nobody else goes down for any significant amount of time. But their injury margin officially shrinks to zero from this point on.

As stated above, this is the one that tips the Oklahoma City boat on its side. You could make a case that it's actually the worst of the OKC blows, and if Wallace were still around to help OKC cover for Williams by committee, I would have it ranked that way.

But OKC losing three rotation wings from last year's roster is too much to absorb Williams and Wallace together. Holmgren is at least going to be back, hopefully, by Christmas or shortly after. Until then, Isaiah Hartenstein and rookie Aday Mara need to hold down the fort, and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander could well end up with his third straight MVP if he keeps OKC afloat during this extended stretch.

That said, it's not going great so far. The Thunder have lost their last two games to Dallas and Houston by a combined 45 points. If the basketball gods have any mercy, they will at least get Alex Caruso (sprained ankle) back in OKC's rotation in short order.

This was originally positioned as a one-week thing. Now we're being told it will be mid-to-late November before the swelling is even expected to be reduced enough to actually assess the situation.

"It's a little bit longer than what people were expecting or hoping," Chris Haynes reported on Oct. 29. "What I'm told is that they have to wait until the inflammation is limited, and then at that point, at the end of that three-to-four-week window, they will assess where to go from there. ... So, a three-to-four-week timetable is what I'm hearing."

Before that update, I was going to force myself to be positive about this one. I told myself, one, it's not the same knee in which Leonard has torn his ACL and MCL, and two, although he did deal with swelling in this left knee last season, it only kept him out a week and he wound up playing 65 games at an MVP level.

I should've known it was too good to be true. If this thing lingers any longer than three to four weeks (which, let's be honest, it's probably going to), Toronto might be able to scrape its way through the regular season, but the expectations of a high seed leading to true championship contention would be out the window. To say Toronto is crossing its organizational fingers is an understatement.

I have this one higher than other injuries that involve longer return timelines for three reasons. First, hamstrings tend to linger, and with Haliburton already coming off a full-year absence from a torn Achilles, Indiana is likely going to play it as safe as possible. This could end up being longer than a few weeks and, as all hamstrings are, it will be a threat to resurface all year.

Second, few teams are as dependent on their star player as the Pacers are on Haliburton, who makes the whole thing go. I'm as big an Andrew Nembhard fan as anyone, but the Pacers with and without Haliburton are entirely different teams. This is like the Pistons losing Cade Cunningham. Maybe worse. If this was officially a longer-timeline return, this would be much higher.

Third, the Pacers have real expectations to contend for a top seed this year, whereas the guys below Haliburton on this list, though out for longer, are not playing for teams with the upside of Indiana, which makes any amount of time Haliburton misses more significant.

Let's hope this is a couple-week thing and Haliburton comes back and he never deals with it again this season (Rick Carlisle did call it a "mild" strain at the outset). But what about the way this season has started across the injury board gives you reason to believe that will be the case?

The Pacers began the season 2-1 but have now lost four straight. They couldn't even beat the Nets, who came in winless, at home on Sunday without Haliburton. If he isn't back by Nov. 13, the Pacers are in major trouble with their schedule: vs. New York, at Philadelphia, vs. Houston, at Cleveland, at New York, vs. Oklahoma City and vs. Philadelphia over the second half of the month.

The Magic might actually be cursed. Two years ago, Banchero and Franz Wagner both tore their obliques, each missing significant time. Last year, Wagner and Jalen Suggs missed a combined 73 games. Over the last two seasons, the trio of Banchero, Wagner and Suggs has played just 25 games.

Now Banchero is out until late November at least, and maybe longer. He didn't even make it two games, going out in the third quarter of Orlando's loss to Minnesota as it opened the season 0-2. The Magic have gone 2-2 without Banchero, and this may not be a death blow if the Magic turn out to actually be better with Wagner operating as a clear No. 1, but his 5-for-20 showing in a loss to Boston on Sunday isn't going to cut it with Banchero out.

We can talk about Banchero's inefficiency and all the issues that come with his Wagner partnership, but he is an apex scorer at his best and he got off to a great start this season with 35 points in the opener. It's hard to imagine the Magic not being a massive hole in a loaded Eastern Conference by the time he gets back.

Remember all the preseason hype around the Jazz? Well, they've started 1-5 and now Jackson is likely out for a couple of months. Utah was getting killed in Jackson's minutes, but there's no denying his importance as a stretch shooter and, more importantly, defensive anchor after the loss of Walker Kessler.

The Jazz have a lot to be excited about on the perimeter with Keyonte George storming out of the gate and Ace Bailey having MIP impact on both ends and the boards (if Darryn Peterson can find his flow, which he will, even better). Brice Sensabaugh is really shooting it.

Unfortunately, the frontcourt hasn't pulled enough weight. Lauri Markkanen has not played well (he could end up traded this season). Kyle Filipowski is taking DNPs. Jusuf Nurkic (foot) is at least expected to make his season debut soon, and that will help a lot, but JJJ being out for a extended stretch is a serious blow to a team already behind the eight ball in a crowded Western Conference.

Grade 2 hammys are a bad deal. They can really linger. Morant was off to a great start with Portland. He and Damian Lillard look like they've been playing together a lot longer than they have. Along with Deni Avdija, they have struck a smooth creation balance. They all lead the offense at different times and are letting it flow when together. Avdija is getting more priority, as he should, as a downhill attacker. Dame isn't shooting it well, but it looks like the old Dame when he forces action off the dribble, and defenses still react to him the same way. He looks pretty comfortable off ball even though the catch-and-shoot numbers are only 36% from 3 so far.

Meanwhile, Morant is, or was, getting into the paint with a controlled aggression. He was coming to jump stops often when he got in there, waiting for the defensive reaction to dictate his next move, be it going up for a touch finish or finding a teammate. He even made 43% of his 3s to start the year. He was genuinely lifting this team in his minutes.

That said, there's a reason everyone thought he should come off the bench to start the year, because even if the fit has been better than expected with Lillard, the Blazers are loaded with guards and therefore should be able to weather Morant's absence.

The Blazers beat the Jazz by 22 in their first game without Morant. Scott Henderson for the start. Jrue Holiday is still there off the bench. Lillard and Avdija can obviously handle the creation; if anything, this clarifies things even more on that end. And the defense should be better with Henderson, Holiday and Toumani Camara seeing more minutes in defensive-oriented lineups alongside Donovan Clingan.

Morant has played well. But Portland is plenty capable of winning without him.

On Oct. 25, the Pistons announced that Duren would be re-evaluated in two weeks. There hasn't been an update since then, so we'll assume that no news is good news and he's on track to return soon. The Pistons need him. A lot is on Cade Cunningham, and these small-ball lineups with John Collins/Paul Reed at the five probably can't be a consistent plan.

But Detroit has managed fine during Duren's absence, winning three of four so far without him; one of the wins even came against the 76ers (albeit without Joel Embiid, which helps when you're playing small) but Detroit was also without Ausar Thompson in that win.

If Duren isn't back in a week, we'll re-evaluate. But so far, Detroit is 5-1 and not in danger of falling into a big hole without its starting center.

The 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is upon us. The Milwaukee Brewers won the belt and the title, and they're now in the process of being feted far and wide. Meantime, an uncertain hot stove season is preparing to unfold. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 1 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

Ace and, for now, back-to-back American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is far and away the most coveted free agent within the current class, and he's almost certain to ink a contract well past the $300 million mark and perhaps the largest contract ever for a pitcher.

On that front, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers, who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a deadline trade; the New York Mets; and the Chicago Cubs are expected to be the leading contenders for the lefty's services, ESPN reports. The Cubs, though, may not be willing to go as high as the Dodgers and Mets may be, and of those two, the Mets at this juncture are expected to be the more vigorous in their pursuit of Skubal.

Now that the Houston Astros have a new general manager in Randy Flores, the attention turns to their current managerial vacancy. Joe Espada's contract wasn't renewed after three seasons on the job.

On that front, current Yankees bench coach and former Tigers and Los Angeles Angels manager Brad Ausmus may be a candidate to replace Espada in Houston and was recently at Daikin Park, MLB.com reports. Ausmus, 57, went 314-322 in four seasons as Tigers manager from 2014-17 and one season with the Angels in 2019. His lone playoff appearance as a manager came in his first season in Detroit. There's a strong Houston connection, as Ausmus was the Astros' catcher for 10 of his 18 seasons in the majors.

The Astros are coming off an American League West title in 2026. However, they finished 81-81 with a negative run differential and were swept in the opening round of the postseason.

#2575. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2574. Cardinals name Gardner Minshew as starter, Carson Beck No. 2: What's next for Jacoby Brissett?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There have been two surprising developments relating to the Arizona Cardinals' quarterback situation following Sunday's dramatic, come-from-behind win over the Dallas Cowboys.

Prior to Sunday's game, Jacoby Brissett was the starter, fellow veteran Gardner Minshew was the backup, and rookie Carson Beck was Arizona's emergency, third-string quarterback. There's a completely new order now.

On Monday, head coach Mike LaFleur announced Minshew as the team's new starter. Beck will move to the No. 2 spot while Brissett is now the third-string quarterback.

The decision to switch starting quarterbacks was surprising enough; LaFleur's announcement that Brissett, the team's starting quarterback for the majority of the last two seasons, was being demoted to the emergency third spot is the real jaw-dropper.

Statistically, Brissett wasn't bad during the season's first seven games. But he struggled against the Cowboys before being replaced by Minshew, who caught fire with three touchdown passes while completing 73.9% of his attempts. Minshew's heroics helped turn a 27-17 deficit with 3:54 left into a 33-30 overtime win. The win improved the Cardinals' record to 3-5.

GARDNER MINSHEW II TO MICHAEL WILSON TO TIE IT LATE📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/t74fyZqpPF

Minshew, 30, has had a roller coaster NFL career. A 2019 sixth-round pick, Minshew started his career in Jacksonville before having stops in Philadelphia, Indianapolis, Las Vegas and Kansas City prior to coming to Arizona this season. His best season was back in 2023, when he earned his first Pro Bowl nod after going 7-6 as the Colts' starting quarterback.

Beck, a 2026 third-round pick, showed potential during this past preseason, going 15-of-19 for 188 yards with a touchdown and no interceptions. His college career included a prolific 2025 season at Miami that ended with an appearance in the College Football Playoff National Championship.

Minshew will make his debut as the Cardinals' starting quarterback next Sunday in Seattle against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks.

LaFleur was non-committal when he was asked about Brissett's future with the team beyond this week. That's usually one of the first indicators (another being a demotion) that a player is likely being dealt.

The Ravens were the first team to come to mind when the news of Brissett's benching broke. Baltimore desperately needs help at quarterback after losing Lamar Jackson to a possible season-ending injury. Backup Tyler Huntley is also expected to miss some time after injuring his toe during Sunday's loss to the Bills, leaving undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano as the only healthy quarterback on the roster.

If the Ravens are going to salvage their season, they need to stabilize their quarterback position as best they can. Brissett would help them do that. He could serve as Baltimore's new starting quarterback or at least be a viable backup for Huntley whenever he is cleared to play.

On paper, a trade between Baltimore and Arizona for Brissett seems easy. The Ravens need a quarterback, and the Cardinals have one they're not using. It could be as easy as that if both teams agree on the trade terms before the league's Nov. 10 trade deadline.

The Cardinals need to be realistic here, though. The Ravens need a quarterback, but they're not going to give away too much for a quarterback who just lost his starting job. Baltimore is also probably realistic in terms of its situation. Without Jackson, and playing in a division where every team has a winning record, the odds of the Ravens doing much this season are slim with or without Brissett, who — if nothing else — could help the Ravens remain competitive.

It would be surprising if the Ravens and Cardinals didn't at least discuss a trade involving Brissett. From the outside, a sixth-round pick sounds fair, or a fifth-round pick in exchange for Brissett and a seventh-round pick. Either way, the Cardinals shouldn't expect to get much in exchange for Brissett, whose time in Arizona has been a disappointment.

#2573. Yaxel Lendeborg continues to revive a Warriors team everyone left for dead

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Warriors fans are losing their collective mind over Yaxel Lendeborg, who continued to one-up himself on Sunday in leading Golden State to a win over the Clippers without Stephen Curry and Draymond Green. It was a completely outrageous performance: 37 points in 34 minutes on 68% shooting, including six 3-pointers.

The rookie added six assists. Threw in four boards and a steal for fun. What this guy has done over his first two NBA weeks is almost beyond comprehension. We're talking about the only rookie in NBA history other than Larry Bird to card at least 100 points, 40 rebounds and 20 assists through his first five games.

His sixth career game was his lone stinker. Luka Dončić gave him a proper hazing. But Lendeborg got right back on the horse on Sunday to become the fourth rookie in history to post 37 and five in a single game on 85% true shooting. Those 37 points are the most scored in a single game by a Warriors rookie since Curry had 42 in 2010, and Lendeborg now ranks as just the third Warriors rookie to average north of 20 PPG (22.3) over the first seven games of his career. The other two are Wilt Chamberlain and Rick Barry. Not bad company.

Yaxel Lendeborg scored 37 points to lead Golden State to victory, the most by a Warriors rookie in a game since Stephen Curry had 42 in 2010.Lendeborg is averaging 22.3 PPG this season, he's the 3rd player in Warriors history to average 20 PPG over his first 7 career games,… pic.twitter.com/T3RgsjFPB9

"That was a huge letdown last game," Lendeborg said of putting his foot in his mouth against the Lakers during his postgame interview. "I just try not to be a letdown again, honestly. I know I've got to keep my confidence no matter what goes on, good or bad game. And I just got to start playing with the joy that I played with the last six years of college and now here. So I'm just continuing to try to keep playing with a smile on my face, maybe throw a little dance move like Steph every once in a while. But I'm gonna just keep trying to find my joy."

Joy is an understatement. This dude's got Dub Nation flying. When I was growing up, there was a great song by Garth Brooks called "Unanswered Prayers," and I thought of it on Sunday as I watched Yaxel burying shot after shot from just about every spot and in every fashion possible, because I'll tell you this: a lot of Warriors fans are thanking the basketball gods that their pissed-off prayers to trade this summer's No. 11 pick fell on Dunleavy's deaf ears.

I mean, look at this guy, in his second week as a pro, chewing the Clippers up like a total 1A alpha.

Yaxel Lendeborg in win vs. Clippers:37 PTS6 AST4 REB13-19 FG6-11 3PTMost points in a game by a Warriors rookie since Stephen Curry in 2010.pic.twitter.com/rSIyjqIEmW

"He's playing this way and he really doesn't know the NBA game yet," Warriors coach Steve Kerr said after Sunday's game. "The game is still really fast for him, but he's so skilled and so talented that he's making all kinds of plays out there. It's remarkable the impact he's having on these games in the first couple weeks of the season."

Look at that reel. This is a rookie who played in just 11 high school games and had to start his career at a junior college taking over an NBA court like a coporate raider. Let's start with the one-on-one scoring, which he's doing in every manner possible: Bullying defenders in the paint, going by them off the dribble, pulling up from 3. Look at these isolation metrics from Tim Legler's All-NBA podcast:

This wasn't just a one-game thing, which, if you've actually been watching and have a functional pair of eyes, you already know. But the numbers are still startling. As further pointed out by the All-NBA pod, Lendeborg is currently the most efficient isolation scorer in the league at 1.52 points per direct play.

When he's not scoring one on one, Yaxel is running the floor like a Hummer or drawing two and dishing. With Curry out, he served as Golden State's point guard, which he noted afterward he's "always wanted to be." He calmed possessions like a veteran. Toggled between pick-and-roll handler and screener. Yaxel did al this while committing just two turnovers, which, during what has otherwise been an almost perfect first NBA impression, has registered as a lone hiccup.

But we have to get back to the shooting. Specifically, the pull-up shooting from range. It's one thing for a guy his size to be a spot-up threat, but this stuff off the dribble, in Kerr's words, "changes everything" in terms of Yaxel's potential.

"We knew he was a good shooter," Kerr said. "When he came in to work out, you could see the skill in terms of being able to put it on the floor and pull up and shoot, but I didn't expect what I saw tonight."

Frankly, you can remove the "tonight" from that answer. Anyone who says they expected anything close to what we've seen from Lendeborg at any point over these first seven games is a stone-cold liar. This dude is giving life to an old, decaying team that everyone left for dead this summer, and certainly after starting the year 0-3. The energy after four straight wins is undeniable. And now you have to wonder if the Warriors' front office has a mind to get aggressive on the trade market rather than waiting for their cap space to open this summer.

Because the simple truth is that Curry remains the best player in the world on any given night. Maybe that fact alone wasn't enough to justify putting the pedal down on this season before Yaxel emerged as a total beast, but now that he has, and with Jimmy Butler set to come back some time after the first of the year, this is a team that can really compete with another piece. They have the Draymond Green and Kristaps Porzingis contracts. They have the draft capital. They have Butler on an expiring deal if they want to go that route. The only question is, do they have the nerve?

#2572. Contemporary Baseball Era Committee unveils eight Hall of Fame candidates: Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown on Monday announced eight candidates for election on the 2027 Contemporary Baseball Era Committee ballot. The non-player ballot includes four former managers and four former executives: Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Lou Piniella, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner, and Bill White.

The non-player ballot includes managers, executives, and umpires. On an alternating basis, the Era Committee also evaluates a ballot consisting of former players. As for the qualifications and criteria, the Hall of Fame describes it thus:

"The eight Contemporary Baseball Era finalists were selected by the BBWAA-appointed Historical Overview Committee from all eligible candidates among managers, umpires and executives whose most significant career impact was realized since 1980. Eligible candidates include managers and umpires with 10 or more major league seasons and retired for at least five years (candidates who are 65 years or older are eligible six months following retirement); and executives retired for at least five years (active executives 70 years or older are eligible for consideration regardless of the position they hold in an organization and regardless of whether their body of work has been completed). All candidates must not be on Baseball's Ineligible List."

As for those figures on the Era Committee ballot for 2027, here's a quick rundown:

Alderson built a powerhouse and won a World Series as general manager of the Oakland A's. He later earned multiple playoff berths and a pennant as GM of the New York Mets.

One of the winningest managers of all time, Baker guided five different clubs to the playoffs and won three pennants and a World Series. His success in the dugout came after a long and distinguished playing career as an MLB outfielder.

Bochy as a manager led three different clubs to the postseason and is one of just six managers ever to win at least four World Series. Three of Bochy's rings came with the San Francisco Giants, and the final one came with the Texas Rangers in 2023.

Maddon won more than 1,300 games as a manager for three different franchises. He also won a pennant as manager of the Tampa Bay Rays, and in 2016, he led the Chicago Cubs to their first World Series title in more than a century.

After an 18-year playing career, Piniella racked up more than 1,800 wins as a big-league manager. He led three different clubs to the playoffs, won a World Series as manager of the 1990 Cincinnati Reds, and in 2001 helmed the Seattle Mariners to a record 116 wins during the regular season.

After filling a key role in the New York Yankees front office, Sabean joined the Giants as their general manager. Under his guidance, the Giants won the World Series in 2010, 2012, and 2014.

The only posthumous candidate on the ballot, Turner owned the Atlanta Braves for two decades. Along the way, he innovated the distribution of televised baseball games and oversaw a dynasty. Under Turner's stewardship, the Braves claimed 14 straight division titles and won the World Series in 1995.

A five-time All-Star and Gold Glove first baseman as a player, White after his playing days were over served as president of the National League. White was also the first Black play-by-play broadcaster in MLB history, and his leadership of the NL made him the first Black president of a major sports league.

The results of the committee vote will be announced on MLB Network at 8 p.m. ET on Sunday, Dec. 6. As with the BBWAA ballot, a candidate must be named on at least 75% of ballots in order to earn election. A 16-member committee will vote on the candidates.

The more traditional BBWAA ballot, in which candidates are voted on by writers and other media members, will be revealed on Nov. 16. Results of the 2027 BBWAA ballot will be announced in January, at which point we'll know the full Hall of Fame class for 2027.

Week 8 concludes on Monday night in Seattle, as the Seahawks (4-3) host the Chicago Bears (5-2) at Lumen Field. Running back Zach Charbonnet, who tore his ACL in Seattle's NFC divisional round playoff win against the San Francisco 49ers in January, is primed to make his 2026 season debut. He doesn't have a game status on Seattle's final injury report, indicating he will be available to play. The situation for First-round rookie running back Jadarian Price is slightly murkier.

Why the lack of clarity with Price's situation? That is because Price, who has missed the last four games with a chest injury while on injured reserve, would need to be activated by 4 p.m. today. Seattle, however, has already designated Price to return with ESPN among those reporting he will play.

"We're going to let the transaction speak for itself on that one," coach Mike Macdonald said.

If the defending Super Bowl champions are going to defeat the high-flying Bears attack led by quarterback Caleb Williams, the Seahawks will need to run the football. Doing so will not only keep Williams on the sideline but also slow down Chicago's pass rush. That second part is key for Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold since he has the NFL's worst expected points added (EPA) per dropback when pressured at -0.63. That's why Seattle traded for Quenton Nelson, and there's a likely chance Nelson will be able to block for both of the Seahawks' top backs in his Seattle debut.

"We have a plan for Zach and with JD," Macdonald said on Saturday. "If we were to make a move, that would happen on Monday to my knowledge. We'll see if that's what we do. We have some things going on roster-wise that we're working through right now, but we have a plan for Zach."

The Seahawks don't have to activate Price on Monday, but they have two more weeks to make a decision on his status before he would be required to move to season-ending injured reserve. On the off chance Price isn't activated for Week 8, Charbonnet would likely share the rushing workload with Emanuel Wilson. Wilson leads the Seahawks in rushing yards (403), rushing touchdowns (three) and carries (111) .

#2568. Eight MLB players tagged with $23.15M qualifying offer: Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Jake Bauers, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight MLB free agents were extended a one-year, $23.15 million contract offer on Monday that, if declined, could fetch their old teams draft-pick compensation. That group includes Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki.

This is one of the smallest groups of qualifying offers ever. Only six players got one in 2020. There were 13 last offseason, and we've seen as many as 20. From 2012 to 2025, 157 qualifying offers were made and only 18 accepted, including a record four last year.

Each offseason, certain free agents are eligible for the qualifying offer (QO). Those eligible free agents have never before received the QO and who spent the prior season with only one team (in other words, players traded during the season cannot receive the QO). The QO is set as the average of the top 125 salaries for a given year, and for the 2026-27 offseason it's a record $23.15 million.

Eligible players who accept the QO will play the 2027 season under that salary for their 2026 team, while those who turn it down become free agents, albeit with the QO compensation attached. That attachment means that the free agent's former team is entitled to an additional draft pick. The position of that draft pick depends upon the team's status when it comes to the luxury tax and revenue-sharing debits or credits.

On the other side, a team that signs a free agent with a QO attached is penalized with the loss of a draft pick, depending again upon the signing team's classification when it comes to the luxury tax and revenue sharing.

Most QO decisions are obvious. Premium free agents receive one without much thought, just as the much less coveted class of free agents do not. It's in the middle ground that interesting decisions lie -- first on the club side and then, if offered, on the player side. That's even more the case this year, when the expiring CBA and negotiations toward a new one have already included talk of a salary cap and restrictions on free agent contracts.

Players presented with a QO this offseason will have until 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to accept or reject the offer.

Below you'll find a rundown of the eight players who received a QO. Do note the players are listed in order of their free agent ranking.

One of the top relievers in baseball over the last three seasons, Morejón gains attractiveness on the open market due to having an effective four-pitch arsenal. That means it's possible he and the team he signs with will want him to convert to a starting pitcher. He could stay in relief, too, where it's likely he'd continue to dominate. A path needs to be chosen, but this guy is a special talent.

Rogers was traded to the Orioles in 2024 and struggled to the point that he needed a trip to the minors. Once he returned in 2025, he was outstanding, pitching to a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts. He struggled to start last season, but made some adjustments and had a 2.90 ERA in his last 20 starts. He's the fallback option to Tarik Skubal, who wasn't eligible for a qualifying offer after a midseason trade.

The power-speed threat posted his sixth straight 20-20 season in 2026 along with an excellent .381 on-base percentage and career-best 5.7 WAR. He's hitting free agency at the right time, though he heads to his age-32 season with sustainability questions, not to mention a few under-the-hood reasons to worry about things going downhill moving forward. Still, it's a weak class for big bats and he'll get paid.

Thanks in large part to huge improvements on defense, Suzuki posted a career-high 5.1 WAR in 2026. His batting average and slugging percentage were right in line with his established career marks and he improved his walk rate to rock a higher OBP. The best path forward is probably to ignore the defensive gains and realize there's a high floor here with the bat for another several years.

There were trade rumors about Jeffers last July, but the Twins hung around in the playoff race and ended up being buyers. Injury limited Jeffers to just 92 games, but on a rate basis he's been a very good hitting catcher for four years, along with being a quality backstop as well.

The NLCS MVP and World Series champion is coming off a career year at the plate. He had a 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR in 144 games and 578 plate appearances, serving as the two-hole hitter for the Brewers throughout the playoffs. He heads to his age-31 season, and this might well be the opportunity of his lifetime for one huge payday.

Lowe just posted a career-high 5.4 WAR in 150 games in his first season with the Pirates, topping 30 home runs for the third time in his career, and he averages 35 homers per 162 games. Are the defensive gains real or a one-year outlier? Will his struggles against lefties prevent a long-term deal?

While there has been some inconsistency (he was brutal for some of 2024, for example), Bednar is coming off a big 2026 season. He was one of the best closers in baseball and showed with the Yankees he can handle a high-profile closing job. He also has a good playoff track record. There isn't much of a top-level closer market in free agency, so he's surely turning this down.

#2566. Luka Dončić explains his 'step forward' on defense after five-steal performance vs. Raptors

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić currently leads the NBA in scoring by an astounding 8.1 points per game, as his 37.7 ppg average dwarfs Tyrese Maxey's 29.6 ppg in second place.

On Sunday night, Dončić increased that average with 45 points (along with 15 rebounds and six assists) in a 131-125 win over the Toronto Raptors, but after the game, much of the focus was on what Dončić did on the defensive end of the floor. Since he entered the league, no one has confused Dončić with an elite defender, but through six games this season, a leaner Luka has looked more engaged and improved on the defensive end for the Lakers.

Sunday night was his best statistical performance yet, as he produced five steals and drew three charges against the Raptors to give the Lakers eight extra possessions that became critical in a six-point win. That effort offered a proof point for Dončić of what he views as a genuine step forward he's taken on defense in his ninth season in the NBA.

"Obviously, I'm not the best defender in the NBA, but I think this year, I really took a step forward," Dončić said (via ESPN). "Obviously, people are going to talk what they want to talk [about] me. ... But I know, and my team knows, that I'm better this year."

Those three charges drawn now tie him for the most in the league this season, alongside Aaron Nesmith, Davion Mitchell, Draymond Green, Jalen Brunson and Keyonte George. He's averaging 1.8 steals per game, which is tied for 15th in the league, and while many will be quick to point out that charges and steals aren't necessarily a sign of great defense, they do point to Dončić's effort level being raised on that end of the floor.

For years, Dončić has been viewed as a one-way player. He is one of the elite offensive engines in the NBA, up in the tier with Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander for the title of best in the world. Defense has never been his calling card, and much of the frustration with Dončić's conditioning is due to a lack of effort on that end of the floor.

This year, Dončić seems to have bought into the importance of showing stronger effort on defense as he takes the reins as the Lakers' leader with the departure of LeBron James. Lakers coach J.J. Redick sees Dončić taking charges as him proving he's taking a step forward as a leader as much as anything.

"I think taking a charge in general is just a form of leadership, right? You're putting your body on the line for the team," Redick said. "... He's trying to win. You see the competitiveness come out so many times on the offensive end, but he's competitive on the defensive end, too."

Between Dončić and Austin Reaves, the Lakers have the potential to be one of the league's elite offensive units. The question coming into the season was whether they could do enough defensively to hold up with a roster that doesn't feature many high-end defenders outside of Walker Kessler.

Through seven games, the Lakers rank 20th in the NBA in defensive rating (113.9). While that's just a bit below league average, for a team with the second-best offensive rating in the league (119.9), it's enough to get the job done. The concern for the Lakers is whether Dončić and the rest will be able to maintain that effort level on defense as the season wears on.

It's easy to commit on the defensive end for a couple weeks coming out of camp, but it's much harder to be locked in 50 games into the season. The Lakers being 20th in the league in defense while touting Dončić's improvement on that end and an increased effort level suggests that if that commitment wanes from Dončić and others, their defense could crash closer to the league's worst units. That would negate the advantage they gain with an elite offense and bring them down a tier in terms of being a contender.

That will be worth monitoring as the season progresses, but for now Dončić and the Lakers are getting a proof point of what they can do when they're locked in defensively. Perhaps most importantly, Dončić is seeing that he can still be an elite offensive player while putting a bit more into his defense, which may make it easier for him to stay committed on the defensive side all year.

For the Lakers to be a threat in the West, the offense has to be elite but the defense needs to simply be serviceable. For now, they've figured out that formula, thanks in part to their star buying in and trying to lead by example with an increased focus on doing the right things defensively.

#2565. Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, more named finalists for MVP, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball, in conjunction with the Baseball Writers Association of America (BBWAA), has announced the finalists for the 2026 major awards: Most Valuable Player, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Reliever of the Year and Manager of the Year.

As a reminder, the voting was completed before the playoffs even started. In fact, ballots were due before the first pitch of the playoffs. That means these are regular-season awards. Further, there's no voting after finalists are announced or anything like that. The word "finalists" is kind of misleading, too. The ballots have already been tabulated and the league office is simply revealing the top three vote-getters for each award to create a buzz before the winners are announced.

Take note that the BBWAA has added a new award this season: Relief Pitcher of the Year for each league. MLB has been naming the Mariano Rivera American League Reliever of the Year and Trevor Hoffman National League Reliever of the Year, but this is the first time the BBWAA has added an award for a relief pitcher.

Monday, Nov. 9: Jackie Robinson Rookie of the Year Awards

Tuesday, Nov. 10: Manager of the Year Awards

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Relief Pitcher of the Year Awards

Thursday, Nov. 12: Most Valuable Player Awards

Yordan Alvarez, Astros: He stayed healthy for a full season and was every bit as good as we all thought he'd be. In 158 games, Alvarez had 34 doubles, 42 homers, 106 RBI, 105 runs and led the majors in all three slashes: .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+). He also led the majors in walks and intentional walks.

Junior Caminero, Rays: At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Bobby Witt Jr., Royals: This is now Witt's fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

Dylan Cease, Blue Jays: In his first season after signing a big deal with the Jays, Cease was one of the few bright spots for the disappointing ballclub. He went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA (184 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 169 innings, finishing with 5.5 WAR. He was the All-Star Game starter.

Parker Messick, Guardians: In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season. Fun fact: Eight pitchers in history have won the Rookie of the Year and Cy Young. Fernando Valenzuela in 1981 is the only one to win both in the same year.

Cam Schlittler, Yankees: Fresh off a great half season and playoffs in 2025, Schlittler just kept impressing. In his age-25 season, he was 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 193 ⅔ innings, holding the Yankees rotation together despite several key injuries. He led the AL in WAR and ERA.

Kevin McGonigle, Tigers: A first-round pick out of high school in 2023, McGonigle made the Tigers out of spring training and took the league by storm. He returned home to Philadelphia for the All-Star Game and finished with an AL-best 7.1 WAR. In 707 plate appearances, he hit .278/.376/.420 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs and 12 steals, all the while playing good defense at both shortstop and third base.

Parker Messick, Guardians: The southpaw got his feet wet in 2025, but the workload was low enough that he maintained rookie status for 2026, during which he excelled. In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season.

Payton Tolle, Red Sox: The 6-foot-6 lefty was a second-round pick in 2024 and debuted last season, though he didn't even work 20 innings and struggled. This time around, he was ready. In 26 starts, he was 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.

Bryan Baker, Rays: After dabbling in relative obscurity for parts of five seasons, Baker broke out at age 31 this year. He led the majors with 41 saves while pitching to a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts in his 62 ⅓ innings for the best team in the AL.

Cade Smith, Guardians: Tied with Baker for the MLB lead in saves with 41, Smith was nails in his first full season as closer. He had a 1.95 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 strikeouts in 74 innings for a playoff team.

Louis Varland, Blue Jays: In his fifth MLB season, Varland really found something and finished with a 1.27 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 97 strikeouts in 78 innings. By late April, he was the Jays' closer, finishing 35 of 37 save chances.

Kevin Cash, Rays: The Rays missed the playoffs in 2024 and 2025 and returned to the Trop after hurricane damage left them without a home in '25. They went out and won 98 games and took one of the toughest divisions in baseball, finishing as the best team in the AL.

Chad Tracy, Red Sox: Tracy took over as manager after the Red Sox got off to a 10-17 start. He went 77-58, making the playoffs. The turnaround featured an absurd stretch during which the Red Sox won 32 of 37 games.

Will Venable, White Sox: Venable became a first-time manager for the 2025 season, taking over a team that lost a modern MLB-record 121 games the previous year. They lost 102 in 2025, but this season improved by 24 games and made the playoffs. This wasn't based much on huge free agency additions or trades for a lot of outside help. It was mostly internal improvement.

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs: We'd seen flashes of the upside before, but PCA put everything together in 2026. He finished a .280/.372/.570 (156 OPS+) hitter with 31 doubles, five triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs and 9.8 WAR. He led the majors in WAR, runs, home runs and led the NL in slugging percentage, OPS and OPS+. He became the seventh player ever to join the 40-40 club, too.

Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers: The four-time MVP looked like he was going to win a fifth for the first half of the season, but injuries caught up to him late. Still, at the plate, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 26 doubles, four triples, 30 home runs, 81 RBI, 89 runs, 11 steals and 3.2 WAR. On the mound, he was 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 85 ⅔ innings with 3.2 WAR.

Brice Turang, Brewers: Nationally underrated, Turang still hasn't made an All-Star Game, though he did start 2026 as a member of Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. In the regular season, Turang hit .268/.366/.450 (124 OPS+) with 37 doubles, three triples, 21 home runs, 100 RBI, 102 runs and 7.3 WAR, rating out as one of the best defenders in baseball.

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers: There was upside to dream on here entering the season and it became a dream season. In 30 starts, Miz posted a 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP and 252 strikeouts in 174 ⅔ innings. He went 16-5 for the team with the best record in baseball and led the majors in ERA, WHIP and strikeouts, among other things.

Chris Sale, Braves: The spindly left-hander won his first Cy Young at age 35 in 2024. He was only able to make 27 starts this season, but he was better in a few rate stats. Overall, he was 14-9 with a 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP and 200 strikeouts against only 31 walks in 162 ⅔ innings.

Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies: Early in the season, Sánchez moved to the front of the line after a scoreless streak of 50 ⅔ innings. At midseason, he started the All-Star Game in Philly. He finished the season 18-7 with a 2.91 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 231 strikeouts in 207 innings. He led the majors in pitcher WAR at 8.1.

Carson Benge, Mets: The 2024 first-rounder made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR.

Sal Stewart, Reds: It's a fight of Old School vs. New School. Stewart only posted 1.8 WAR, but he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The last eight players to do so won Rookie of the Year. The only ones who didn't win came before there was an award or someone else did it in the same season (two rookies in 1950 got to 30-100).

JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals: Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and help push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Jhoan Duran, Phillies: In his first full season with the Phillies, Duran closed down 33 of his 35 save chances with a 1.82 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 84 strikeouts in 59 ⅓ innings.

Mason Miller, Padres: In 70 innings across 66 appearances, Miller pitched to a 1.67 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and struck out 129 hitters. He won five games and converted 38 of his 41 save chances.

Trevor Megill, Brewers: Though the Brewers didn't always employ a traditional closer, Megill was the closest thing to it, securing 30 saves in 33 chances with a 2.63 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 69 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings.

Don Mattingly, Phillies: Mattingly started the season as the bench coach before taking over a 9-19 team for the fired Rob Thomson. Immediately, the Phillies got hot. They ended up going 79-55 under Mattingly, making the playoffs yet again despite starting 10 games under .500.

Pat Murphy, Brewers: Managers almost never win this award in back-to-back seasons because it's generally given to the guy whose team most exceeded expectations. How could that possibly happen two straight years? Well, Murphy now is going for three. In 2025, the Brewers set a franchise record with 97 wins and had the best record in baseball. In 2026, they set a franchise record with 103 wins and had the best record in baseball.

Walt Weiss, Braves: In 2025, the final season of Brian Snitker's career, the Braves were a disappointing 76-86. Weiss was hired in the offseason and went 94-68, getting the Braves back on top in the NL East after a two-year hiatus.
